transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi... yeah, it's nice to meet you too. Um, well, I guess I'm here because things have just been really, really hard at work lately. I'm a hairstylist—I work at this salon, mostly doing color and cuts, which I usually really enjoy, you know? I've been doing it since I finished my associate's degree. But recently, I don't know, it's like my body just isn't cooperating with me anymore. 

It’s the weirdest thing. My hands literally feel like they’re moving through thick glue. Like, just the basic stuff that I usually do on complete autopilot... even just sectioning a client's hair with my comb before a cut, or standing in the back room mixing the color and the developer in the bowl... it just takes me absolutely forever now. I'll be standing there trying to stir the color and it's like I'm moving in slow motion. It takes so much physical effort just to do the normal motions. 

And it’s not just me feeling it, either, because people have actually started noticing. My coworkers and my manager, they've been giving me these looks, and a few of them have pointed out that I’m just way slower than I used to be. Which is incredibly stressful because in a salon you have to stay strictly on schedule, you know? You have clients booked back-to-back, and if I'm taking twenty minutes just to prep a section that used to take me five, it throws the whole day off for everyone. I just... I can't seem to speed my body up no matter how hard I try to force myself, and I don't understand why I'm like this all of a sudden.

Yeah... yeah, I guess that’s exactly what it is. It’s just this constant... weight. Most days, honestly almost every single day lately, I wake up and before I even open my eyes, I just feel this heavy, flat sadness sitting right in the middle of my chest. It’s like an actual physical pressure, almost like someone set a cinderblock right on my ribs while I was sleeping. 

I’ll just lie there in bed staring at the ceiling, listening to my alarm go off on snooze again and again, and I just can't find a single reason to push the covers off. I used to be the kind of person who loved getting my day started. I'd get up and make my coffee and think about which clients I was seeing that day, or what new balayage techniques I wanted to try out. But now... it just feels like there is absolutely no point in trying to build the life I was planning. 

I had all these goals, you know? I wanted to build up my own solid book of regular clients, maybe rent my own chair in a high-end place, or even open a little boutique studio space eventually once I saved up enough from working at the salon. I had this whole timeline mapped out in my head the day I finished my associate's degree. I was so driven. But now, with that heavy, flat feeling every morning, it all just feels so useless. Like, why even bother? Why try to build this career or this life when everything just feels so incredibly empty? I just look at my shears and my styling station now and I don't feel any of that old excitement. It's just this overwhelming sadness, and it stays with me all day, just dragging behind me while I'm trying to force myself through my shifts.

A tremor? Like, my hands shaking? Um, no, no I haven't noticed anything like that at all. Honestly, if my hands were shaking, I think I would be the first to know, just because of what I do for a living, you know? When you’re holding incredibly sharp shears right next to someone’s ear, or you're trying to paint a really precise foil or a highlight right up to the root without bleeding the color onto the rest of the hair, you have to have absolutely steady hands. 

And my hands are steady. They really are. I was actually just looking at them the other day when I was doing a long layered cut on this client who’s been coming to me since I first got my associate's. I was holding the comb and my shears, and I was just staring at my fingers, and they were perfectly still. They just... they just don't want to move *fast*. It's not that they're trembling or jerking around or anything. It's just that awful, exhausting heaviness I was talking about. Like they're weighed down by lead. So yeah, definitely no shaking, my hands are totally still... they just won't go when I tell them to, which is almost more frustrating because I know exactly how to do the cuts, my hands know all the angles, they just refuse to cooperate with my brain.
Have you noticed any stiffness in your muscles?

Stiffness? Um, no, I don't think so. I mean, my muscles don't feel stiff or tight or anything like that. It's really just the slowness. Like I said, it's that heavy feeling, like I'm trying to move underwater or through thick syrup. But they don't feel rigid, you know? 

Like, when I'm reaching up to blow-dry a client's hair, my arms don't feel locked up or anything. I can still reach up and move the brush around and everything, it's just that it takes so much effort to lift my arms up in the first place, and then to keep them up there while I'm working the round brush. And blowouts are already hard work, you really have to pull the hair taut to get it smooth, especially if they have curly or textured hair. But my joints and muscles themselves, they feel fine. They're not tight or cramping up. 

I actually stretch quite a bit, too. In cosmetology school, they drill it into you that you have to take care of your body because standing on your feet all day and holding your arms up can really take a toll. So I'm always stretching my wrists and my shoulders between clients. And I haven't noticed any difference in my flexibility or anything when I do my stretches. It's really just the lack of energy, that awful dragging sensation. It's not that my body *can't* bend or move, it's just that it feels like it doesn't *want* to.
Have you been feeling unusually sensitive to cold?

Cold? Um, no... no, I don't think so. I haven't really noticed anything like that. 

I mean, the salon where I work is always kept pretty chilly, honestly. It's just because when you have, like, six different blow dryers going at once, plus curling wands and flat irons that are set to 400 degrees, and everyone's ring lights are on, the room heats up so incredibly fast. So the owner always keeps the AC cranked up to compensate for all the hot tools. My styling station is actually right near one of the main overhead vents, too, so I'm pretty much always standing right in the draft while I'm working. 

And, you know, our dress code is all black—which is standard for most salons so you don't ruin your clothes with bleach or color—so I usually just wear a short-sleeve black tunic or a cotton t-shirt. If I was suddenly super sensitive to the cold, I feel like I would definitely be freezing and shivering all the time standing right under that vent. But I feel totally normal temperature-wise. 

Even when I'm back at the shampoo bowls and the water inevitably splashes down my arms, it just feels like regular room air hitting wet skin, nothing extreme. My roommate actually keeps our apartment like an absolute icebox at night, too. She has this window unit in the living room that she just blasts, and I still just sleep with my normal, everyday comforter. I just lie there under it in the mornings, feeling that same awful, heavy weight I was telling you about earlier... but I'm not actually cold. So, yeah, physically, my temperature regulation seems completely fine. I haven't needed extra sweaters or anything like that.
Before this current period, have you ever had another episode of depression like this?

Another episode? Like... before this whole thing started? Um, no. No, I haven't. I mean, I've had bad days, obviously. Everyone has bad days. Like when I was in cosmetology school, there was this one week where I completely botched a color correction. It was supposed to be this beautiful, seamless balayage, and it ended up looking so banding and brassy, and my instructor totally tore me apart in front of the whole clinic floor. I went home and cried for, like, three hours and I didn't want to go back the next day. I felt so stupid and useless, like I was never going to get my associate's and I'd wasted all this money. 

But that was just... that was just a bad week, you know? It passed. I went back, I practiced on a mannequin head until my fingers cramped, and I got over it. It wasn't anything like *this*. This is... this is totally different. 

Before all this started, I was actually doing really well. I was building my book at the salon, getting a lot of repeat clients, and I was even thinking about asking the owner if I could start taking on some of the bridal parties that come in on weekends. I had all this energy. I'd work a ten-hour shift, on my feet the whole time, doing blowouts and full foils, and then I'd still have the energy to go out with my roommate or try out a new styling technique I saw on Instagram. I loved what I was doing. 

So, no, I've never felt this... this heavy, dark, awful feeling before. Never. It's like someone just flipped a switch and suddenly everything is just so incredibly hard. I've never been through anything like this in my entire life.
